source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024) Eliciting the Priors of Large Language Models using Iterated In-Context Learning
finding: Method to read out an LLM's prior: iterated in-context learning. GPT-4 predicts, data is sampled from the prediction, the model sees the data, and the loop repeats until the chain settles on its prior.
numbers: 100 chains (4 seeds x 25 starts), 12 iterations, temperature 1. Causal strength chains converged at iteration 7 (generative) and 8 (preventive).
limits: Assumes the LLM acts like an approximate Bayesian agent; not proven. Human comparison is visual, from published figures.
agent_relevance: A prior can be measured from the model instead of asked for. Our S0 gate could measure the model's own prior by sampling, then compare it with the class record.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024) Eliciting the Priors of Large Language Models using Iterated In-Context Learning
finding: On causal strength, the empirical GPT-4 prior fit GPT-4's judgments best on correlation, but a uniform prior was close. Preventive case: empirical prior had higher r, uniform had lower RMSD.
numbers: Generative: Pearson r uniform 0.85, sparse-and-strong 0.79, empirical 0.86; RMSD 0.21/0.25/0.19. Preventive: r 0.72/0.68/0.79; RMSD 0.26/0.29/0.27.
limits: Small gap between a uniform (indifference) prior and the elicited prior. Sample sizes 8, 16, 32 only.
agent_relevance: Indifference priors are not much worse here, but the elicited prior is never worse on correlation.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024) Eliciting the Priors of Large Language Models using Iterated In-Context Learning
finding: On everyday quantities (lifespan, movie grosses, poem length, Pharaoh reigns, runtimes, cake times) GPT-4 priors matched human priors in the mode but differed in shape, notably for Pharaohs.
numbers: Six tasks from Lewandowsky et al.; convergence in roughly 2 to 11 trials. No numeric correlation with humans reported.
limits: Visual comparison only.
agent_relevance: Model priors on common quantities look human-like, so a base-rate check against the class record is a fair test of where the model's prior is off.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024) Eliciting the Priors of Large Language Models using Iterated In-Context Learning
finding: On speculative events, direct questions gave vague or apologetic answers, but iterated learning gave concrete prior dates.
numbers: Median years: superhuman AI 2042, zero carbon 2045, Mars colony 2050; convergence in 5, 5 and 9 trials.
quote: The distributions recovered from GPT-4 suggest the model has plausible priors for these speculative events.
limits: Plausibility is the authors' claim; no ground truth exists.
agent_relevance: Sampling reveals priors that a direct prompt hides; direct prompts for unknown quantities may hit refusal habits.

source: Selby et al. (2025) Had enough of experts? Quantitative knowledge retrieval from large language models (Stat 14:e70054)
finding: LLM-elicited priors for effect sizes differ a lot by model. Most centred Cohen's delta near 0.2-0.25; GPT-4 centred near 0.5. Spread (effective sample size) also differed by model.
numbers: Models: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Mistral-7B, Llama 2 70B. Mistral gave Student-t nu=30 every time; Llama-70B-Q5 gave nu=5. Mistral sometimes gave alpha >= 1000.
limits: Temperature 0, zero-shot, single agent. Comparison with six human psychologists is in figures only.
agent_relevance: Prior strength is a model-specific trait. A measured class record should override the model's own prior width.

source: Selby et al. (2025) Had enough of experts? Quantitative knowledge retrieval from large language models (Stat 14:e70054)
finding: Prior-data conflict: LLM weather priors were often so confident or wrong that a frequentist model needed almost no data to beat them.
numbers: 25 cities, December temperature and precipitation vs Open-Meteo; effective sample size often near 0. Slight bias toward larger, more populous cities.
limits: Exact values not in the text.
agent_relevance: Overconfident priors are a real risk. Record the measured outcome next to the model's guess and trust the record.

source: Selby et al. (2025) Had enough of experts? Quantitative knowledge retrieval from large language models (Stat 14:e70054)
finding: Data leakage: models recognised public datasets, which contaminates tests of elicited knowledge. Imputation by LLM mostly lost to mean/mode, KNN and random forest.
numbers: Of 11 datasets GPT-3.5 identified 6, Gemini 1.5 Pro 5, Llama 2 70B 2. Talis case: GPT-4o coefficient 0.618 (95% 0.380-0.850) vs baseline 0.738 (0.401-1.066).
limits: 64 OpenML-CC18 datasets (abstract says 50). Only one hierarchical case study. No measured sample-size saving; the 500% figure is a hypothetical.
agent_relevance: Be careful: a model's 'prior' may be memorised data. Do not count it as independent evidence.

source: Capstick, Krishnan & Barnaghi (2024/2025) AutoElicit: Using Large Language Models for Expert Prior Elicitation in Predictive Modelling
finding: AutoElicit asks an LLM for priors on linear model weights, then refines them with natural-language guidance. Priors cut labelling needs versus an uninformative prior.
numbers: Synthetic: about 10x lower test MSE after 5 examples, matched by 20. UTI dementia data (78 people, 371 labelled days): same peak accuracy after about 15 labels, saving over 6 months of labelling. Bayes factor favoured AutoElicit on all datasets.
limits: Linear models only. UTI dataset is private. GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4-turbo, DeepSeek-R1-32B tested at temperature 0.1.
agent_relevance: Closest existing use of an LLM prior inside a pipeline. Gains come from a good prior plus small data.

source: Capstick, Krishnan & Barnaghi (2024/2025) AutoElicit: Using Large Language Models for Expert Prior Elicitation in Predictive Modelling
finding: Failure cases: GPT-3.5's in-context predictions did not match its own elicited prior, and weak models returned uninformative priors when unsure.
numbers: Energy-statistic gap between in-context and elicited prior: UTI 0.39, Heart 0.18, Hypothyroid 0.15, Diabetes 0.38, Breast Cancer 0.31. In-context learning gave linear predictions on only 2 of 5 datasets. Heart Disease: GPT-3.5 matched uninformative prior only.
limits: Memorisation of public data possible (appendix tests). Only the first 100k characters of the page were read.
agent_relevance: The model does not reliably use its own stated prior. Make the prior an explicit written object that later steps must use.

source: Anon (2025) How many patients could we save with LLM priors?
finding: LLM hyperpriors for a hierarchical adverse-event model gave only tiny gains over meta-analytic priors, and the headline claim is overstated.
numbers: 468 patients, 125 sites. Best: Llama 3.3 blind T=1.0 LPD -3.842 +/- 0.294 vs baseline -3.963 +/- 0.464. 80% data with LLM prior -4.093 vs 100% with baseline -4.103 (about 66 patients). MedGemma blind T=0.5 was -4.133, worse than baseline.
limits: Differences inside the SDs; no significance test; best config picked on same data; disease-informed prompts did not beat blind ones.
agent_relevance: Do not take LLM-prior gains at face value. Measured data beats elicited belief.

source: Huang (2025) LLM-Prior: A Framework for Knowledge-Driven Prior Elicitation and Aggregation
finding: Framework where the LLM writes parameters of an explicit prior, and several priors are pooled by a logarithmic opinion pool.
numbers: Coin with 8 heads, 2 tails: Beta(1,1) -> posterior mode 0.800; Beta(5,5) -> 0.667; Beta(18,2) -> 0.893. Pool of Beta(1.60,1.40) and Beta(1.50,2.00) = Beta(1.55,1.70), mean 0.477.
limits: Proof of concept. Visual checks, no benchmark, no uncertainty on LLM output, no prompt-robustness study.
agent_relevance: Shows the context of the prompt sets the prior; so the prior is whatever the prompt says. Pooling several priors is a cheap robust option.

source: Atwell et al. (2025/2026) BASIL: Bayesian Assessment of Sycophancy in LLMs
finding: A framework that elicits the model's prior, likelihood and posterior and checks whether the stated posterior follows Bayes' rule from the model's own prior. Stating the user's belief moves answers much more than the same belief from a third party.
numbers: Models: gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, phi-4-14b, Mistral 7B, Llama 3.2 1B and 3B. Tasks: conversation forecasting, morality, cultural acceptability. Mistral 7B had most Bayesian error; size did not predict rationality.
limits: Small and mid models; self-consistency is the standard, not ground truth. 'Hybrid' elicitation gave much more error than direct probing.
agent_relevance: Priors should be fixed before the user's view arrives (S0 gate), otherwise the answer follows the user.

source: Atwell et al. (2025/2026) BASIL: Bayesian Assessment of Sycophancy in LLMs
finding: Fixing the prior alone makes things worse. Calibrating the prior and then rescaling the posterior with an odds ratio cuts Bayesian error. Fine-tuning for Bayesian consistency also cut error and sycophancy.
numbers: Calibrating priors only raised Bayesian MSE; calibrating prior plus scaled posterior reduced it (significant, Fig. 3). BayesSFT used 600 examples (200 per dataset); BayesDPO ranks by closeness to own Bayesian posterior; both reduced error on Llama 3.2 1B.
limits: Exact MSE values are only in figures. Tested on small Llama.
agent_relevance: If the agent changes a prior, it must carry the change through to the posterior step. Never swap a prior silently.

source: Dual Traits in Probabilistic Reasoning of Large Language Models (2024)
finding: Frontier models do Bayes correctly when all numbers are given, but fall back on similarity (representativeness) when base rates must be recalled.
numbers: Structured test, Q4: state-of-the-art models 1.0 vs humans 0.20, affordable 0.10, small 0.16. Hard item Q10: 0.39. Jason problem (base 75% vs 25%): normative odds ratio 9; GPT-4o 9, GPT-4 9, Llama-3-70B 9, Claude-3-Opus 8.86, Gemini-1.5-Pro 6.36, Mistral-Large 3 for uncharacteristic text.
limits: Metalinguistic prompts only; closed models; human benchmark mismatch (normative 5.44 vs reported 2.25). RLHF explanation is a conjecture.
agent_relevance: The prior is the weak step when the model must recall it. Put the base rate in the context, do not ask the model to recall it.

source: Dual Traits in Probabilistic Reasoning of Large Language Models (2024)
finding: With representative descriptions the base-rate shift vanished. In the unstructured test, posteriors tracked similarity, not priors.
numbers: Representative descriptions: ratios near 1 (CS 1.18-2.58, humanities 1.00-1.60). Adam test: prior-posterior r about -0.88 to -0.95; posterior-similarity r about 0.90 to 0.98 (7 rotations per question).
limits: Small sample; Fisher z used.
agent_relevance: Models reproduce base-rate neglect in the same direction as humans when the description is vivid.

source: Dual Traits in Probabilistic Reasoning of Large Language Models (2024)
finding: Wording matters a lot: changing 'indicate' to 'compute' raised GPT-4o's base-rate use. Four stronger Bayes-rule prompts did not remove the similarity bias in the unstructured test. Recall was the main problem: GPT-4o stated a prior of 2-4% when asked directly but used 10-30% during posterior judgment.
numbers: GPT-4o ratio rose from about 1.25 to about 9.5 (CS) and 1.04 to 8.5-11.7 (humanities). Prior-posterior r stayed -0.75 to -0.94 with explicit prompts.
quote: LLMs struggle to recall base-rate information from memory
limits: One model for the prompt study.
agent_relevance: Force explicit step by step compute and write the prior number down once, then reuse it.

source: Metacognitive Myopia in Large Language Models (2024)
finding: Argues that LLMs show base-rate neglect as a symptom: output is drawn from training text conditioned by the prompt, and missing cases (for example 'I don't know' answers) are not counted in the base rate.
numbers: Conceptual paper, 71 pages; no new effect size. Example: code answers exist for common queries, absent for rare ones, so 'no answer' is never learned.
limits: Theory and argument, not a measured experiment.
agent_relevance: Our agent needs an explicit record of failures and misses, since the model's own sample leaves them out. This supports the class record.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Benchmark with a family on base-rate and probabilistic reasoning among judgment biases. Its background section cites earlier findings that GPT-4 shows base-rate neglect and conjunction fallacy at rates like humans, CoT partly helps, and natural frequency formats reduce neglect in LLMs.
numbers: Downstream evaluation lists 25 benchmarks (section heading). Cited: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi 2024; Lampinen et al. 2022; Dasgupta et al. 2022.
limits: I read only the background and taxonomy text; the main result tables were not extracted. Cited claims are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Present priors as counts (n out of N), not percentages.

source: The Base-Rate Effect on LLM Benchmark Performance: Disambiguating Test-Taker Strategies from Benchmark Task Performance (2024)
finding: A different base rate: models carry a prior over answer labels (A-D). Accuracy on MMLU depends on how likely the model finds the correct label before reading the question.
numbers: Cloze zero-shot: GPT-2 got 0.007 on questions where A is never correct but about 0.33 elsewhere. Mistral Nvr-A 0.273 vs Nvr-D 0.512; SOLAR 0.503 vs 0.625. LLaMa3 stable (0.560-0.629). Counterfactual prompting lowered but did not remove it.
limits: Zero-shot only; models up to about 10B.
agent_relevance: Shows hidden priors in the model bias answers. Randomise option order and test with it removed.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs do not update beliefs as a Bayesian would across rounds; fine-tuning on a Bayesian Assistant's outputs fixes much of it and transfers to new tasks.
numbers: Flight recommendation, 5 rounds, 624 simulated users, 48 human participants (improved round 1 to 5, p = 0.002). Fine-tuned models agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time. Bayesian teaching beat oracle teaching on hotel and web shopping transfer. Assistant uses a uniform prior; other priors performed similarly (appendix).
limits: Exact accuracies only in plots. Only three mid-size open models fine-tuned.
agent_relevance: A uniform prior was good enough here, so an indifference start is fine if updates are done correctly. Updating, not the start, was the weak part.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock & Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Telling a model to start from a base rate improves forecasts slightly; telling it to reason Bayesian makes them worse. Most prompts do nothing.
numbers: Study 1: 38 prompts, Claude 3.5 Sonnet/Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B. After correction only Frequency-Based Reasoning (diff -0.019 Brier, adj p 0.022), Base Rate First (-0.016, adj p 0.036) and Step-Back (-0.015, adj p 0.036) helped; Bayesian Reasoning (+0.025, adj p 0.036) and Propose-Evaluate-Select (+0.028, adj p 0.010) hurt.
quote: references to base rates yield slight benefits
limits: Effects tiny; combined prompts in Study 2 (with o1, o1-mini) gave no significant gain (e.g. Base Rate First + Frequency-Based -0.012, adj p 0.162). Authors suggest the Bayesian prompt leads to mimicry.
agent_relevance: Put base rate first, in plain frequency terms. Do not write 'be Bayesian' in the schema.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval-based LLM forecasting system comes near the human crowd; retrieval matters most. Models hedge toward the middle.
numbers: 914 test questions. System Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149; 4:1 blend 0.146; best zero-shot GPT-4 0.208; random 0.250. Ablation: base GPT-4 no retrieval 0.206 vs with retrieval 0.186. Calibration RMS error 0.42 vs crowd 0.38.
limits: SEs assume iid; small category samples; selective-setting results chosen on validation. No separate base-rate ablation reported though prompts ask for base rates.
agent_relevance: Evidence beats the prior; the loop gets better by finding evidence, not by a better prior prompt.

source: Paruchuri et al. (2024) What Are the Odds? Language Models Are Capable of Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: Models can estimate percentiles and probabilities of known distributions, with large errors zero-shot; examples and context help; a plain normal approximation often beats CoT and code.
numbers: Percentile MAE: GPT-3.5 25.7%, GPT-4-Turbo 14.9%, Gemini 1.0 Ultra 16.5%. Adding one in-distribution example improved by +59.14% (percentile). Gemini real-world: normal approximation 5.89-7.62% vs CoT 6.45-10.48%.
limits: Skewed or long-tailed distributions are worst.
agent_relevance: Shape of the prior matters; give the agent the class record's counts, not a guess.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022/2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Models, like people, reason better when content fits belief, which is a hidden prior at work. CogBias cites this work for natural frequency formats reducing LLM base-rate neglect.
numbers: Only abstract read: three tasks (NLI, syllogisms, Wason). No numbers on the page.
limits: Abstract only; the base-rate claim is from CogBias citing this work, not checked in the paper itself.
agent_relevance: Believability can leak into logic; ask for the check without the story.

source: Jaynes (2003) Probability Theory: The Logic of Science; Bertrand (1889) paradox
finding: Objective-Bayes machinery (maximum entropy, indifference) is the human-side background. Not opened this session.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Background, not read.
agent_relevance: The LLM literature above shows a uniform start is rarely the problem; neglect of recalled base rates is.

source: Lampinen et al. (2022) cited by CogBias: chain of thought partly mitigates probabilistic errors
finding: Second-hand claim only: CoT partly but not fully fixes probabilistic reasoning errors.
numbers: None.
limits: Cited in CogBias, not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat CoT as partial help for base-rate use.
